analysis.evidence: אַךְ introduces an exception to the preceding permission to eat animals. The prohibition לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ applies to flesh with its life, identified here as its blood, still in it.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected restrictive particle with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: only, except, however (limiting what was just said)

analysis.evidence: בָּשָׂר is the object of לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ, “you shall not eat.” The phrase בְּנַפְשׁוֹ דָמוֹ specifies that the prohibition concerns eating meat with its lifeblood still in it.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: meat, as food and in sacrifice

analysis.evidence: The prohibition concerns eating בָּשָׂר, “flesh,” with its life. The next word, דָמוֹ, “its blood,” stands in apposition to נַפְשׁוֹ and identifies the life in view with the blood.
analysis.morphology: The preposition בְּ means “with.” The common noun is of common gender, singular and in the construct state before the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix וֹ, “its.”
analysis.sense: the life that is in the blood

draft.change: Add Genesis 9:4 as defining evidence for the existing sense blood-of-a-living.
draft.definition: The blood of a living creature, identified here with its life.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 9:4, דָמוֹ identifies the life mentioned in בְּנַפְשׁוֹ as the creature’s blood.

analysis.evidence: דָמוֹ stands in apposition to נַפְשׁוֹ in בָּשָׂר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ דָמוֹ, “flesh with its life, its blood.” The matching suffixes refer to the same creature. Its blood is what the prohibition לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ forbids eating with the flesh.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix וֹ, “its.”

analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: בָּשָׂר ‘flesh’ is the object of תֹאכֵלוּ. The clause לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ forbids the addressees to eat flesh with its lifeblood.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine plural. The preceding לֹא makes the clause a prohibition.
